This review is for those with experience playing Path of Exile 2; new players are encouraged to play the game to develop their own opinions.

To be clear, Path of Exile 2 has the potential to evolve into something great… the greatest ARPG ever in fact. Even small design shifts like the introduction of a dodge roll have added substantial tactical depth to the gameplay. But despite these improvements, the game’s publicly stated design philosophy is increasingly at odds with the actual gameplay experience. 

GGG has repeatedly insisted that PoE2 is meant to be slower and more deliberate. That’s a fine vision; but in reality, endgame mapping and enemy speed blatantly contradict this claim. The pace remains just as frenetic as it was in PoE1 and there’s just as much onscreen effects which can make it exceedingly challenging at times to even know what’s going on. If the intent was to slow things down, then loot distribution should have been adjusted to match. It hasn't been. On the contrary, this current iteration has made currency even more scarce, doubling down on grind without commensurate reward. The trade system? Still a disaster, faithfully carried over from PoE1 with all its archaic inefficiencies.

GGG seems unwilling to internalize a lesson that should be fundamental by now: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. Many systems are saturated with negative modifiers that drain momentum and morale rather than inspire mastery. Nowhere is this more obvious than in end game mapping, where stacking mods can paradoxically make a map less playable due to sheer mechanical overkill. Several mods outright mean that if you luck into the wrong map suffix you will automatically be throwing that map in the trash (I’m looking at you temporal chains).

Yes, the game is in early access, but GGG seems to have misunderstood what early access is for. It’s supposed to be a testing ground, a sandbox for players to explore systems, theorycraft, and search for broken interactions. In a  game that’s loot dependent, that requires access to resources. Instead, loot is miserly. I constantly run over 100% magic find and still see abysmal returns. Divines are rare. Exalts bizarrely drop more often than Chaos, Regals, or Alchemy orbs. Orbs of Annulment or Chance? Nearly mythical (I say this after playing for over 420+ hours).

Crafting is nonexistent in any meaningful form as the entire system has been reduced to pure gambling. The tools are there and were shown to work in PoE1, but in PoE2 there’s no actual semi-deterministic crafting so experimentation dies on the vine. 

Defense stats in PoE2 remain deeply imbalanced. Armor is still underwhelming, scaling poorly in the face of high incoming damage. Evasion is serviceable. Meanwhile, energy shield continues to dominate across most content. This persistent asymmetry undermines build diversity and reinforces a stagnant meta. This is further exacerbated by the aforementioned lack of currency and crafting, which often leaves players stuck if they’re not wealthy enough to regear their characters in a different manner.

The Trial of the Sekhema is one of the more baffling screwups in the game. The central mechanic, an “honor” meter that diminishes when you’re hit, actively punishes entire archetypes of play. Builds that rely on taking damage as part of their identity such as anything melee related, thorns-based, armor-heavy, or self-damage synergies, are effectively penalized for functioning as intended. The concept of "honor" in combat might make sense thematically, but from a gameplay perspective it's incoherent. “Oh but honor isn’t an issue if you stack honor resist”, ok, stacking “honor resist” is a lazy workaround, not a solution. “Well you can do the Trials of Chaos then”, sure, let’s talk about the ToC.

The Trials of Chaos continue the trend of stacking punishment under the guise of difficulty. Layer upon layer of negative modifiers are applied to both the player and the environment, creating scenarios where success often feels less like a result of skill and more like surviving Jonathan’s spite. Once again, the issue isn’t that the trials are difficult, it’s that GGG confuses misery with difficulty. These trials don't challenge a player's decision-making or adaptability so much as test their tolerance for suffering. Some of the modifiers will 100% of the time be a death sentence, which is ridiculous for a game mode that demands you run a gauntlet.
To reiterate: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. And until GGG takes that distinction seriously, much of the game's potential will remain unrealized beneath the weight of its own contradictions.

And then there’s the death penalty: a flat 10% XP loss. It’s an outdated design relic that punishes players disproportionately, especially in a game this unstable. The optimization is rough; CPU usage spikes inexplicably, screens freeze, and enemies with invisible on-death effects can wipe you before you even register the threat. The game already limits player through currency scarcity and map restrictions, why stack another misery mechanic on top of it all? Literally nearly every one of my high level deaths has been due to the game freaking out and freezing for a split second at the most inopportune times. This is the mechanic that makes me rage quit. This is the mechanic that makes me put the game down and leave it for extended periods of time. This is the mechanic which makes me rethink spending money on stash tabs, cosmetics, mystery boxes, etc.

Let me be absolutely clear here: the XP penalty is not just frustrating, it’s demoralizing. It actively discourages continued play and reveal a fundamental disrespect for player time. Once you hit the late 80s or early 90s in level, even fully juiced maps roll several levels below your character level, making XP grinding a slog. Combine that with PC performance issues and what you’re left with is a bad experience. And yes, I can already hear the diehard fanbase trotting out the same tired defense: “There have to be consequences, otherwise people will just spam content and they won’t learn how to get good.” Sorry, but no. That argument falls apart under the most basic scrutiny. Players can’t spam the same content; maps are gated behind RNG & limited runs. The system itself is already self-limiting. You don’t need an additional punitive XP penalty to “preserve challenge”; you need a well-balanced game that respects player time and rewards effort instead of eroding it in a hot instant.

Things I would like to see:
• Campaign Skip After Completion
Once a player has completed the campaign, they should be allowed to skip it on subsequent characters. 
• Make the Remaining Campaign Choices Reversible
In both Act 3’s, characters are forced to make two decisions regarding stats that are currently permanent. This design is incoherent, especially given that ascendancy choices can now be changed freely. Please allow these decisions to be changed as well (Let Doryani be the interface to make the changes).
• League Character Imports
The requirement to re-run the campaign for each new league or character is, again, tedious. A solution could involve importing characters back into a new league; either starting fresh at level 1 or with a baseline (e.g., level 60 with 500k gold and access to early maps). 
• PoE1 Atlas Skill Tree
The Atlas passive tree in PoE1 was amazing. The current iteration in PoE2 is by comparison a poor imitation. Bring back that depth!
• Boots: movespeed is necessary, so make it an implicit
• An Actual Early Access Philosophy: Treat the current state as a live experiment, not a soft launch. Be generous with currency, unique’s, and loot bases (hell let Ketzuli have another few tabs that just sell white bases), focus on testing systems rather than preserving some arbitrary economy that can easily be reset or wiped.

It pains me to write this review but I have no choice. 

Right now, the game is not worth your time. Why? Because it OPENLY disrespects your time. I have over 700 hours, and let me be honest, I would say at least 500 of those hours feel like a complete waste. The campaign is just great. Extremely punishing, stupid difficult, but overall pretty fun. The gameplay does feel slow and methodical, and the bosses are a solid blend of challenging but doable. 

However, when you get to maps, and then as you push through beyond level 85 (I made it to level 96), the game becomes completely different. It's much less methodical, everything either kills you instantly or you kill it instantly, and there is virtually no in-between. There are like 5-6 builds that are mandatory to progress, so build-diversity is zero. 95% of the uniques are completely and utterly worthless. And worst of all, every death comes with such an OVERWHELMING amount of punishment, that your literal life force as a human will be drained. Beyond level 70, you lose 10% XP per death, which is absolutely INSANE beyond level 95. Every death will wipe DOZENS and eventually HUNDREDS of hours of character XP progress. It got to the point where every death was an instant log off and do something else moment. You lose, the map, you lose the node modifiers, you lose all the loot on the ground, and you lose 10% XP. I have never before experienced a game so punishing with every death. 

In its current state, the game is simply NOT fun beyond the campaign. Every moment is so stressful because the amount of stupid 1-shot mechanics with zero telegraph or counterplay is just insane. So many deaths you won't have a CLUE what killed you. And again, keep in mind the cost of every death. This combination makes the game essentially unplayable. 

I am hopeful for the game's future. But for now, I am out.

Games are supposed to be FUN not so fucking tedious and boring. I don't understand why they didn't seem to learn anything from their 10 years of running POE 1. It actually feels like they took a few steps back.

I’d purchased Early Access under the impression that this game would scratch a longstanding itch—which is to say that while there has been, in my mind, a trend of oversimplification across games of several genres, this one would offer depth and meaningful character-building.  Whereas other games gave (and continue to give) merely an illusion of choice, PoE2 would allow me to lose myself in all the different possibilities its system would offer.

For the duration of version 0.1, the game met those expectations.  The campaign was (and still is) 200% more time-consuming than it needs to be, but I found a very fun and comfortable endgame loop: run some maps, tinker with my build, maybe find a different mechanic or ability to explore, maybe change my build entirely (which likely entails re-gearing), rinse, repeat.  I brought four characters to level 90+, thoroughly fascinated by what each of their classes brought to the table in terms of distinctiveness—and intrigued further yet by what magic sometimes happened when, say, I took one class’s ostensible predispositions and superimposed them on some aspect(s) of a different class’s identity.  This constituted a freedom rarely seen anymore in character-building systems.

And then it was gone.  The 0.2 update saw an end to all of that by way of imposing arbitrary limits to the skill tree; the developers saw what they labeled as overpowered builds, and instead of fine-tuning the numbers/skills/options to rein in those builds—or, indeed, enabling [i]other[/i] possible builds to reach the same heights—they gutted the system.  (baby:bathwater::fun:unbalance)  Now, as with seemingly every other game, there’s merely an [i]illusion[/i] of choice; while the skill tree is large and visually full of possibilities, there are only a few and finite number of viable ways to play a given class.

That has been my primary gripe since the 0.2 update, but the game is imperfect in other ways.  (See: the numerous other negative reviews here; see also: the complaints on the GGG message boards.)

[b][i]“Bro, the game isn’t done yet.”[/i][/b]


^This is a frequently touted rejoinder to criticisms of the game, and while it’s very true that the game is still in Early Access, this trite remark does not take into account what has happened.

Imagine you’re watching a baker of some renown prepare a cake for you.  You’ve already paid for your share of the cake, and you—like the many others who have invested—intend to eat your own share.  This master baker creates the batter with some basic ingredients: flour, eggs, milk, sugar.  He throws in some cinnamon, vanilla, maybe something more unconventional, like miso. So far, so good.  Then he throws in some dogshit, shredded cardboard, and ground horseshit.

“The cardboard is an interesting choice,” a fellow customer says.  “But can we forego all the shit?”

The baker waves a hand dismissively.  He says, “The feces is part of the vision.”

“Bro,” another customer says.  “The cake isn’t done yet.  Let the man cook.”

Oh, he’s absolutely right: the cake isn’t done yet.  [i]But the baker has intentionally just thrown shit into the batter.[/i]


As far as I can tell, the “vision” GGG is pursuing is the much-maligned, never-much-played “Ruthless mode” of PoE1.  I wasn’t around for PoE1; I had to read about this failed experiment more recently.  Arguably, I played its most recent iteration.  I don’t like it.  I love a challenge, but that’s not what this game is.  On a fundamental level, this speaks to a core issue with the game’s current state: the developers appear to have conflated [i]challenging[/i] gameplay with [i]annoying[/i] gameplay.  After having wasted so much time on player trades that ultimately fell through, I see the lack of an auction house as the best example.  The game’s archaic trade system has players manually reach out to other players for gear the latter have made available for sale; far more often than is reasonably acceptable, trades fall flat.  From what I understand, the “vision” prescribes some measure of “trade tension”, the expectation being that a player feels a greater sense of relief(?)/elation(?)/accomplishment(?) when a trade successfully results in a gear upgrade—absolutely ludicrous.  See also: excessively large maps, experience loss on character death, extreme scarcity in useful loot, invisible one-shots, etc, etc, etc.  In keeping with this design philosophy, they could make players solve a prolonged series of CAPTCHAs before they’re allowed to log in: fire hydrant, crosswalk, bus, bus, motorcycle, fire hydrant, fire hydrant, traffic light, bus, bus, bus, bus, bus, bus, motorcycle…  Pass the images through a dark fantasy filter and boom, “challenging” gameplay!  

The bottom line is that GGG is making this game as slow and as cumbersome and as otherwise artificially “challenging” as its player base will allow.  If that’s your jam, then shit, more power to you.  Me, I can’t recommend this nonsense—even after all the time and money I’ve put into it.  [i]Especially[/i] after all the time and money I’ve put into it.

Reader, I uninstalled it.  I’ll likely check back every now and then, though to be clear, the bullshit present in the game is there [i]by design[/i].  Maybe we’ll see something closer to 0.1 after the dust settles, but I’m nearly certain we will not.

Path of Exile 2 delivers deep character customization, challenging combat, and a much stronger campaign experience than most action RPGs. The visuals, boss fights, and skill system are impressive and rewarding for players who enjoy experimenting with builds. However, the game can feel overwhelming for newcomers, and some progression and balance issues are still noticeable during early access. Overall, it’s a very promising ARPG with excellent gameplay depth, but it may require patience and a willingness to learn its complex systems.

[b]Path of Exile 2 has the potential to become one of the best action RPGs ever — but right now, in early access, I do not recommend buying it.[/b]

I’ve played PoE 2 for over [b]1,000 hours[/b] in its first year of early access, and I don’t regret the time — but the experience has been increasingly frustrating, and in its current state I don’t think it’s a fair or stable experience for new players.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Economy Is Not Optional[/h2]

PoE 2 is a game that — in my experience — can only be enjoyed properly if you meaningfully participate in the in-game economy. To do that effectively you need premium stash tabs and especially AFK shop tabs. Without them, trading efficiently is difficult, risky, prone to scam attempts, and time-consuming.

Community creator GhazzyTV once described Path of Exile as:

[quote]
“Free to try, not free to play.”
[/quote]

That still applies to PoE 2.  
Meaningful economy participation costs additional money.
Plus, PoE 2 early access costs money straight away! It will only be [i]"free to play"[/i] on full release.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Fate of the Vaal – Economy Collapse[/h2]

The most recent Fate of the Vaal league exposed how fragile the economy can be. A new league mechanic — the Temple — was poorly balanced at release, and an abrupt rewards increase just before a holiday break caused massive inflation. By the time GGG returned and patched the situation, many players were so far behind they could no longer participate meaningfully. A league intended to last ~4 months became effectively unplayable after about [b]1 month[/b] for a large portion of the player base.

GGG did not:

[list]
[*] Roll out a patch quickly  
[*] Reset the economy  
[*] Roll back progress  
[*] Punish exploiters  
[/list]

The situation was justified with “it’s early access.”

Technically true. Practically devastating.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Community Response Says Everything[/h2]

The community organized and crowdfunded a private league called:

[b]Second Wind: Fate of the Vaal[/b]

[list]
[*] ~51,000 total slots  
[*] ~48,000 registered players  
[*] One of the largest private leagues in PoE history  
[/list]

Tens of thousands of players voluntarily paid to join a community-run reset league because they wanted:

[list]
[*] A fresh economy  
[*] A fair start  
[*] A playable league  
[/list]

That level of participation speaks louder than any forum post.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]There Are Good Things[/h2]

To be clear:

[list]
[*] Combat feels good and challenging  
[*] Build depth is promising  
[*] Core systems have real potential  
[/list]

But none of that matters when:

[list]

I really enjoyed the campaign gameplay, story and the flexibility of how I could build my characters. This continued until around level 70 when I finished the last of the campaign and started the mapping grind. Once I started the endgame grind I figured this would be when I started being able to really min/max my character, experiment with builds and really dial things in gear-wise. Sadly this was not the case, instead I started to discover just how many little (and sometimes not so little) time sinks have been designed into the game. Everything, inventory management, UI/UX design, buying/selling items, building up enough currency to buy items, finding citadels on the map, literally every aspect of the game’s design is engineered to hold your time hostage and then for some of it they offer to ransom it back to you for real money. Some will argue that you can play the game without spending a penny and they would be right, you can. However the game is specifically designed to make that choice hamper your gameplay in every respect. 

Beyond the design elements that attempt to ransom your time back to you there are elements that just unapologetically thumb their nose at it. For example player deaths and the 10% XP loss. At level 70 this is no big deal and you won’t think much of it. Once you reach the upper 80s and into the 90s you are going to start losing hours and hours of gameplay and it just gets exponentially worse. For me this was most common when mapping with friends and 9 times out of 10 I wouldn’t even be able to see what killed me and maxing out resists does not guarantee you won’t still get one shot by something you never even saw coming. The level of visual noise is so incredibly high that it just isn’t possible to see everything that could kill you. I can live with it when it is my mistake and I just got lax. When the player is not given the opportunity to try and avoid it then it becomes a design flaw.

Player to player item sales early on were ok, it was quick, efficient and most players were polite enough to let you know if the item you DMed them about was currently being sold so you didn’t waste your time waiting on them to respond. Over time a shift took place and people stopped communicating and the process became a lot of refreshing the page waiting for the market to update so you could see if they sold the item to someone else. Instead of being able to just pay an intermediary system this system requires the player to be online, it requires the player to stop what they are doing to meet up and it requires that you don’t miss a message in your chat log which is very easy to do when mapping. It seems like it was perhaps designed to push players to engage with each other but unfortunately it winds up being just as impersonal as an automated marketplace and far less efficient. It even goes so far as to clash with mapping mechanics. When you generate a map with a waystone you get a limited number of portals to access the map. Every time you leave the map and go back it consumes a portal. Due to limited inventory space it is very easy to consume most or all of your portals just retrieving loot. Leaving a map to meet with a player and sell an item will consume one of these portals making it the wise choice to finish the map first which can often result in a missed opportunity to sell something as the buyer often hedges their bets by DMing multiple sellers with similar items.

Ascension trials are terrible. Period. The honor mechanic in Sekhemas punishes melee classes while making it easy by comparison if you are ranged. Trial of Chaos will often present you with such terrible debuff options that synergize with each other so strongly you can wind up forced into an unbeatable trial. It should always be possible to get through it! This is another place where the game can completely waste your time and provides absolute nothing but frustration in return.

The list of problems this game has goes on but I’ll just conclude by saying that if you value your time and don’t want to invest in a game that has no respect for the limited time we all have on this earth then look elsewhere for your entertainment.

Updated review after spending 200+ hours. I've forced myself to go through most of the endgame, pushed to t15 maps, got lvl 90, 8 ascendacy points etc.

While there are moments of greatness, significant flaws hold the game back from being truly enjoyable in the long run. 

Pros:

Animations are fluid and visually impressive, adding a sense of polish to combat and abilities. Same with effects and graphics in general—the world of the game is visually appealing, with a great atmosphere that does it job to immerse players into the dark fantasy world of POE.

The 3-Act campaign is well-crafted, enjoyable, and easily the most rewarding part of the game.

Cons:

Endgame Balance: The endgame feels tedious, plagued by poor drop rates, frustrating atlas mechanics, and build limitations. Progression feels more like a chore than a reward. Tldr: You might end up crippling your experience and getting frustrated faster than you may get your 5 socket gem or find your first divine orb :)

On-Death Effects: These mechanics are far too punishing and unfun, making the game feel unfair rather than challenging.

RNG Dependency (in a bad way): The trials (Sekhemas and Chaos) are overly punishing. The mechanics lack inspiration and offer little room for meaningful counterplay. The RNG itself is too punishing—if you get unlucky with debuffs, you can outright lose the trial through no fault of your own. For example, getting a movement speed debuff often leaves you as good as screwed, no matter how well you’ve prepared. I think it can be easily improved by adding more links between room choices in Sekhemas and more debuff choices in Chaos and making debuffs less punishing at least in early stages.

Similarly, the Atlas system feels like a battle against RNG rather than a test of skill or preparation, punishing players regardless of their gear or build. The endgame allows little to no creativity in build crafting. The game is so punishing that players are forced to build around strict defensive caps just to survive. For example, you have to push resistances, but even then, you can still be one-shot by an absurd "on death" mechanic from a random white mob. Survivability becomes mandatory, leaving players no choice but to roll defenses on every single piece of gear. The game is just unplayable otherwise.

*Kripparian’s video "Path of Exile 2 is Ruthless" captures these issues perfectly. The endgame systems feel needlessly harsh and punishing.

Final Thoughts (updated):

I can recommend Path of Exile 2 in its current state solely for its excellent 3-act campaign, which is a fantastic experience.

However, I suggest avoiding the game’s endgame content for now, as it is plagued by poor balance, frustrating RNG mechanics, and punishing systems that stifle build creativity.
If you’re interested in the good endgame experience, I recommend waiting until GGG hopefully addresses at leat some of the abovementioned issues, fixes the endgame, adds more classes, updates the skill tree, fixes armor/resistance balance and so on. But as it stands, I can’t recommend playing endgame in its current state, nor am I willing to overlook the game's flaws simply because it is "better than Diablo 4." Being better than a bad game is hardly an achievement, and Path of Exile 2 should aim much higher.

⚔️ [h2]1. Combat Overhaul: Tactical Genius vs. Brainless Zooming[/h2] ⚔️
For over a decade, ARPG combat was defined by running at lightspeed and evaporating screens of monsters with a single button. [i]Path of Exile 2[/i] completely shatters that paradigm.

[h3]WASD Controls & Dynamic Animation Shift[/h3]
The inclusion of [b]WASD movement[/b] alongside traditional click-to-move is a total game-changer. It gives the game a highly responsive feel that allows me to kite, dodge, and aim abilities independently of my movement vector. Coupled with a dedicated [b]dodge roll mechanic[/b] featuring conditional frames of invulnerability, combat is a skill-expressive dance.

[h3]The Diablo 4 Contrast[/h3]
Compare this to [i]Diablo 4[/i]. In D4, combat quickly evolves into a repetitive loop of management metrics: I pull an entire room, spam my resource-generator, execute a core skill, and wait for cooldowns while level-scaled mobs melt into screen-wide visual clutter. In PoE2, [b]every single skeleton matters[/b]. Standard trash mobs can easily punish lazy positioning, and the [b]50+ campaign bosses[/b] are massive, multi-phase mechanical encounters reminiscent of [i]Dark Souls[/i]. I cannot simply out-gear a boss; I have to learn their attack tells and master my animation locks.

+-------------------+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+

Build-crafting is where PoE2 utterly decimates [i]Diablo 4[/i]. Blizzard restricts my identity: if I play a Necromancer in D4, I must use Necromancer skills, and only you can hold a shield.

PoE2 retains the brilliant, fluid class philosophy of its predecessor: [b]any class can use any weapon or skill gem[/b] if they meet the attribute requirements. Early Access introduced gold as a tangible currency, fixing a historical hurdle. I can spend [b]gold at NPCs to easily respec passive skill tree points[/b]. PoE1 felt like the game handed me a huge box of parts and said, “see what you can make.”
PoE2 feels like it hands me the same box with a rulebook attached.

I understand the balance philosophy, but for me that restraint comes at the cost of experimentation, build identity, and the sheer fun of creating something stupidly powerful and weird.

Path of Exile 2 Review – A Diamond with Rough Edges

Path of Exile 2 improves upon its predecessor in many ways, offering deep ARPG gameplay with stunning visuals and smart QoL upgrades. However, several frustrating design choices hold it back from greatness.
✅ The Good: Why PoE 2 Shines
[list]
[*]Clearer & Smoother Progression
        The revamped skill tree and leveling system are more intuitive than PoE 1, making builds easier to plan without sacrificing depth.
        Passive skill choices feel more impactful, and early-game pacing is improved.
[*]Graphics & Atmosphere
        The game looks gorgeous, with detailed environments, improved lighting, and a distinct art style that sets it apart from other ARPGs.
        Monster designs and spell effects are visually striking (even if sometimes overwhelming).
 [*]QoL Improvements
        Reconnect feature is a game-changer—no more losing progress due to crashes or disconnects.
        Alva’s Currency Exchange shows the potential for a better trade system (now we just need it for everything else).
 [*]Endgame Potential
        The core gameplay loop (maps, bosses, loot hunting) remains addictive, and new mechanics add fresh challenges.
[/list]

❌ The Bad: What Needs Fixing
[list]
 [*]Post-Death Effect Overload
        Killing mobs shouldn’t feel like navigating a minefield, yet PoE 2 insists on filling every encounter with delayed explosions, lingering ground effects, and stacking DoTs. In Delirium, this becomes absurd—waiting 20+ seconds after clearing a pack just to avoid death isn’t engaging gameplay; it’s tedious. The visual clutter makes it worse, as effects blend together, leaving players guessing where to stand.
 [*]Corridor Hell: Lack of Open Maps
        The endgame map variety is shockingly bad. Out of dozens of maps, only four (Savannah, Oasis, Rustbowl, Steppe) feel truly open. The rest are claustrophobic tunnels or obstacle-filled pseudo-open zones (looking at you, Creek and Blooming Field). Maps like Augury, Decay, Hidden Grotto, Seepage, and Vaal Foundry are outright miserable, forcing players into repetitive, cramped combat.
 [*]Ranged Combat Feels Punished
        The game pretends to support ranged builds but constantly forces point-blank engagements. Mobs burrow, teleport, or materialize out of thin air, nullifying the advantage of distance. Shadow creatures, underground ambushes, and off-screen projectiles make ranged play feel like a lie.
  [*]Outdated Trade System
          The trade system is stuck in 2013. Alva’s Currency Exchange proves that automated trading works, yet the rest of the economy relies on:
  [list]
         [*]Mandatory third-party tools (Awakened PoE Trade, trade sites).
         [*]Being online 24/7 to sell items. As a result trade market was crowded with bots and price fixers until game lost 70% online.
         [*]Constantly leaving maps to complete trades.
         [*]It’s a time-wasting relic that favors no-lifers and punishes casual players.
  [/list]
      Solution: Expand Alva’s automated trading to all items.
  [*]Crafting = Gambling
          The crafting system is a slot machine disguised as depth. Want a top-tier item? Prepare to:

This is going to anger a lot of POE fans, but I want to preface this with saying that I have always been more of a Diablo player. I enjoy its more simplistic nature that doesn't require a degree in statistical mathematics to get the most out of. The screen clutter was also a big turn off in POE and just looked ridiculous to me. I am glad to say that some of these "problems" from my view have been addressed in POE 2, to a certain extent. 

The game is a lot slower and more methodical than the average ARPG; it feels almost souls-like in some parts. It's a very different style compared to the rest of the genre, and certainly to POE 1. Which is also the reason why the game has garnered a lot of hate from fans of the first game. I personally love this new direction and had a blast playing the campaign, as far as it's available right now. Endgame is another matter - here the game fell flat on its face for me. Suddenly I was confronted with the mapping system, which ditches every aspect of the game I enjoyed until then (that being the story, the goal-oriented map design, the progression in biomes, the leveling and powering up of my character and frequent game-changing gear upgrades) and replaces them with mindless, practically zero progress grind in completely randomized, context-devoid fighting arenas. I would have thought that it was a placeholder for early access, if I didn't know that POE 1 employs a similiar system. It gets ridiculously punishing as well, to a draconian degree. Suddenly monsters hit like ten times harder and beat you into the muck in fractions of a second. The screen clutter also gets much worse, too often conceiling one-shot capable projectiles or monster death effects underneath. And every death is brutally punished by the game by taking away your XP (the few scraps you even get at this point) and your ingredients used for opening maps. This ain't a difficulty spike, this is a difficulty SPIRE.

And yeah, the fans of the first game are going to say "this is where the fun begins!" but I have neither the time nor the desire to play this game 24 hours a day for a month straight just to make a single level of progress and find a weapon that does .1% more damage. 
POE 2 by no means stands alone in this, almost every ARPG has the same kind of decline towards the end, requiring ungodly amounts of work for nearly no benefit; but here the contrast couldn't be starker. So while I fell in love with the game's style and gameplay during the main campaign, as soon as that ended, so did my fun. And yes, I realize that the endgame is optional, and I can simply choose to not engage with it. I can still criticize it though. 

What's left is a game that has two faces: one that invites me in with its exhilerating gameplay, intense grimdark style and narrative, and one that angrily shoos me away for not sacrificing my entire life to the grind. I can only hope that the first face gets some love from the developers too.

Good foundation ruined by "The Vision"

POE 2 has infinite potential, but is completely bogged down by the GGG's stupid vision of what they want the game to be.
They want two contradictory design philosophies to exist within the same game, causing it to be a schizophrenic, inconsistent mess of a game.


It is obvious that GGG wants the game to be a hardcore, slow paced dodge game, where enemy hits matter and damage cannot be tanked easily, but this kind of design only works when the difficulty of the game is consistent and predictable, a game where you fight a few enemies at the same time at most, so that you can respond to attacks and look for openings in enemy movesets. A game where you learn the timings of enemy attacks, learn what attacks you can take, poise through, etc.   Basically a Fromsoft game.

What the community seems to want though, including me, is a fast paced, screen clearing, blasting gameplay. Killing hundreds of enemies at any given time. The kind of gameplay where your whole screen being covered in visual effects is a good thing and not a death sentence.

This game tries to have both. You are always facing entire screens of enemies that have the potential to one-shot you at any time, which doesn't work together well and ends up punishing you for not seeing one big attack inside a complete garbled mess of visual effects caused by:
your abilities covering half the screen if you're playing the game correctly, 
enemy attacks and modifiers covering the screen in VFX, 
stupid amount of ground effects that most maps will have
dozens of on death effects that enemies leave as well as other random league mechanics like delirium or breach which add another layer of visual clutter to an already incomprehensible mess of effects


GGG wants this game to be difficult, which is fine, but the way they do it is not fine at all.
Enemies do a lot of damage as a baseline which is done to make combat "meaningful", which would be perfectly fine in a game with consistent difficulty, but this game does not have that.

This game has modifiers that you add to maps as a whole that make monsters stronger or you weaker, modifiers that monsters spawn with randomly which can stack up into a short novel under the monster's name, modifiers that give other enemies buffs, shrines that buff monsters around them, spirits that possess monsters to give them even more buffs
This combined with the baseline monster damage and the eye cancer that is covering the screen at any point in time, results in a completely inconsistent, unbalanced and ultimately frustrating experience, filled with random one-shots that you don't learn anything from, as most of the time, you will have no idea what killed you.

All of this is made worse by the fact that death is also heavily punished, you lose XP, lose your map, lose the charge of expensive tablets, causing even more frustration and friction that is completely unnecessary, but GGG seems to think punishing=hard and hard=good.
This extends to a lot of features in the game, even simple convenience features like sprint are punished heavily if you make the mistake of taking even the tiniest hit during it, causing a very long stun and basically certain death if there are any enemies near you when you fall.

I don't mind games being difficult, learning from mistakes and overcoming difficult challenges can be very satisfying, but being randomly kicked in the nuts every 30 minutes by a monster moving at mach 3 speed with the whole Lord of the rings trilogy written under it's name, that hits you for 3 times your health total is not particularly fun or engaging, nor do I learn anything from dying that way, I just get that much closer to completely dropping the game every time.

I see the potential in POE 2, I know there is a great game somewhere under all these poor design choices, which is why I sunk over 500 hours into it just this season, but the more I play, the more frustrating these design issues become.
This alongside the myriad of bugs that are constantly bricking league mechanics, costing me time and resources, that stay unaddressed for weeks or months, would make me not recommend this game in the state that it is in now. I doubt that the design philosophy will change drastically at any point, but if it does, POE 2 has the potential to be an incredible experience

There is a lot to like about this game, even in its current early access state. The visuals, story, and combat are all excellent. WASD control and roll dodge add a lot to the experience. On the surface everything appears to signal a winner. However, once you scratch past the surface you quickly realize this game still has a long way to go before it is ready for a broader audience as outside extreme enthusiasts and those with many hours a day to invest, it is not a rewarding experience AT ALL.

First of all, there is NO progression system in the game. None at all. 100% of the so-called "crafting" system is a gambling casino slot machine simulator with tiny modifiers. You take a random drop with 1 or 2 decent stats on it, and use an item that "removes one random stat to add X." That means you have a very good chance of removing the valuable stat and rendering the half decent item totally worthless. That is a best case scenario. The vast majority of crafting items literally just "remove a random stat to add another random stat" or "add a random stat" or "upgrade to a rare item with 4 random stats." 90% of the time this results in useless trash and wasted resources and most important, TIME.

On the subject of time, I have never played a game that has less respect for your time. Currency needed to play the crafting slot machine mini-game is EXTREMELY stingy with drops. I can run half a dozen fully juiced t15 maps with 3 tablets plus Doryani for +1 level irradiated (20 or 30+ modifier maps) and not get ONE single Divine Orb. Couple this with the obvious and rampant RMT currency buying going on that GGG seems to have no interest in policing. Literally many of the top build guides on Youtube are overtly advertising buying cheap in-game currency for real money!

The "league" system is also terrible for the average player with maybe a few hours a day to invest. Due to the aforementioned stinginess of loot drops and rampant cheating/currency purchasing, the economy is absolutely broken after the 2nd or 3rd week of any given league. The items needed just to run an effective build for t15 endgame maps for even a hope at the stingy currency drops is driven up to many hundreds or THOUSANDS of Divine Orbs (as of this review ONE Diving Orb trades for over 600 Exalted Orbs), with some individual items being multiple thousand Divine Orbs and yet, the drop rates are awful. Maybe one per map if you are lucky.

So, the only people this game seems designed for is those who can afford to stay at home and grind for 12+ hours a day to maybe have enough currency to buy the gear they need to "progress" after several weeks of hair pulling tedium/madness, cheaters who simply buy currency for real money on one of the many dozens of websites advertising openly on Youtube and build guide sites, or gambling addicts who enjoy the thrill of repeatedly wasting days of their life grinding currency on the hopes they will one day "win the jackpot" of actually gaining a useful item, which they often won't even use but just sell to recoup some of their losses.

The game has so much potential to be great, but GGG appears to be married to this Las Vegas style RNG gambling casino slot machine loot system. There is ZERO progression system, ZERO sense that by investing time your character gets stronger proportionally. There is ZERO respect of your time as a player. On top of this, the only cosmetics are cash shop items with an average outfit price of $30 to $40. That is a big ask considering the "vast ocean 2 inches deep" level of effort they have put into making the game feel like it rewards you for your investment.

In its current form it is a fun game for the first few acts, but endgame is the epitome of "all stick, ZERO carrot." For days or weeks of your life invested, you literally have nothing to show for it except maybe a few more pulls at the slot machine. An absolutely HORRIBLE design married to RNG for ALL loot that is unfortunately destined to fail. But, I would recommend playing the first few acts at least. It is a fun combat experience. Hopefully GGG can do something about the worthless economy and utter lack of meaningful rewards apart from an occasional gamble token.

Before diving into the negatives, I have to admit that I never played Path of Exile 1. However, I was constantly told how complex and deep the game’s mechanics were. POE2 is supposed to simplify things, but I was still led to believe how challenging and intricate the game would be, particularly the skill tree and crafting. That made the endgame loot and crafting all the more disappointing.

Cons:

- The loot filter is essential. Unfortunately, it’s not integrated into the game and has to be downloaded and installed from a third party. This isn’t a big issue on PC, but I still think it’s weak that it’s not handled through in-game menus. What do console players think about this?

- Many long-time POE players will hate me for saying this, but their beloved trade website is nothing more than an external auction house. This, too, isn’t integrated into the game, and I have to use a website to trade. This should absolutely be part of the game itself.

- Trading currently only uses two currencies: Exalted Orbs and Divine Orbs. Boring. Many, including myself, have often criticized Diablo 3’s in-game auction house, especially POE players. And even if no one wants to hear it – yes, the POE trade site is an auction house. Period.

You set your loot filter and wait for a blue or yellow item with decent stats. There are no useful unique items to get excited about – most are dismantled right away. Everyone just waits for a God-tier yellow item to drop so they can sell it on the auction house to buy their own God-tier item. There are no sets, no runes, and no rune words. Is this supposed to be the incredible loot system? Blue and yellow items?

- Crafting in POE means applying orbs with random effects to items and hoping for the best. Sure, it feels good to roll great stats once in a while, but it’s not really engaging.

I only mention the skill tree because every POE player immediately points to how massive it is and what you can supposedly do with it. Almost as if they're trying to compensate for something.

All in all, it's a good game, but the boring loot and the utterly uninspired crafting system personally ruin the fun for me. The omnipresent auction house, aka "the trade site," which isn’t integrated into the game, along with the external loot filter, drives me away for now.

I can't remember the last time I gave a game a negative review. Honestly, I don't want to give this game a bad review either. I want to like POE2. In fact, I am happy to recommend it later if enough things change. My problem is that, at the moment, the game has too many mechanics that are intentionally designed to prevent you from succeeding unless you get lucky.

There are typical video game barriers that are meant to be overcome where the solution is fun and learning. POE2 requires that from you, but asks for so much more; giving you opportunity, then taking it away without offering you the chance to try again. Did an Atlas Map boss defeat you? Congrats, you can never fight that boss again, forfeiting their loot (which includes more Atlas Maps). Did you get one shot, with 4000 shields, from the perfect combo of Rare Modifiers on a monster right out of the gate? Congrats, you didn't just lose the XP in that Atlas Map, but you lost XP from the last 2 Atlas Maps you completed as well. Did really rare currency drop for you, but you immediately died from invisible ground damage? Too bad. It's gone and there are no "escape death" skills available in the game.

It is understandable that people would make the "Git Gud" argument. I don't necessarily disagree, but what concerns me is that getting "gud" in POE2 isn't fun and involves a lot of RNG. Around level 90 the game just doesn't feel fun anymore and most, if not all, of the endgame activities do not have sustainable mechanisms to help players recover from unfortunate experiences without demanding more time, more risk, and other sacrifices...

I don't have a lot of time to play video games. The holiday season is an exception. The last thing I want is to put an hour into a game only to be worse off than when I started. It's okay to slow progression upon failure, but to take it away feels cheap and un-fun. Video games should be an escape and feel rewarding. Even if I did plow through all of the challenges to hit max level, I don't believe I would feel like the time was worth it. And, I would certainly not want to go through that pain again with multiple characters; potentially one I might like more.

I told myself I would review the game after hitting level 90 to give it as fair of an assessment as possible. There are things I love about POE2, but the endgame, as is, does not want me as a player. As an engineer myself, I have a bunch of ideas I'd bring to their brainstorming sessions, but I know I'm just one player. If you are like me then I cannot recommend POE2 until GGG values our time better or until it fully releases for free.

[h1][b][u]My Ongoing Journey with Path of Exile 2![/u][/b][/h1]

Early Access Struggles: The Noob Chronicles

Prior to this Early Access, I played around 70 hours on the original game, give or take a few dramatic rage quits, and let’s just say my experience wasn’t exactly award-winning.

I jumped into Path of Exile 2 with zero expectations; I knew from the start it wasn’t going to be easy. So imagine a hyperactive cheerleader with zero rhythm, that’s basically me trying to master this game. I died a lot. Like, embarrassingly often. Bosses turned me into a pincushion, and my build? A glorified paperweight that barely did any damage early in my playtrough.

Grinding, Building, and Finally Winning

After a lot of trial and error, and countless rage quits, I discovered the magic formula: patience, persistence, and a bit of luck. Building a decent character in PoE 2 is like assembling IKEA furniture blindfolded, frustrating but oh-so-rewarding when done right.

Once I landed on a working build. ... 😈

the gears started turning. Bosses got less deadly, and leveling felt like progress instead of punishment. The game’s notorious difficulty softened a bit, and I even managed to snag some wins that felt legitimately earned. Not bad for a guy who used to die just opening a chest.

Updates and Endgame: Smooth Sailing… Kinda

Fast forward to recent updates, and things have eased up, mostly because my character’s a tanky beast now. Grinding the early game over and over gave me a leg up, and the new content didn’t feel like an insurmountable wall.

That said, the endgame is still a beast. Hardcore players will have their work cut out for them, and the trading system remains a maze I haven’t fully navigated. For me, it’s casual grinding and occasional boss fights, and that’s perfectly fine.

Trading, Community, and the Hardcore Divide

Let’s be real: I’m not the trader king or hardcore min-maxer. I mostly play for the fun of the journey and rely on community tips to avoid faceplants. PoE 2’s player base is brutal but also incredibly supportive if you stick around and ask questions.

If you’re a hardcore PoE veteran, this might feel slow or shallow. But for casual players like me, it’s a wild ride that rewards perseverance more than perfection.

Final Thoughts: Still Challenging, Still Worth It

Path of Exile 2 isn’t a walk in the park. It’s more like a hike up a mountain wearing flip-flops. It’s tough, unforgiving, and sometimes downright confusing. But when you finally conquer a boss or figure out a build, it hits that sweet spot of accomplishment few games can match.

Will I keep playing? 

Hell yes. Despite all the chaos and frustration, this game scratches an itch no other RPG does. Just don’t expect to be good right away, mess up, get roasted, level up. Repeat.

My first ARPG, and I have to say it was totally worth it. I still have a lot to learn and my builds are probably a mess, but thanks to all the guides online, I've been managing just fine. It's been a really fun experience so far!

(Disclaimer: I know I'm a few hours shy of the 3,000 required to have a valid opinion on this game (and its predecessor), so if you're a longtime PoE veteran, please forgive my utter hubris in posting this review. I'm sure seeing a disgusting casual like me must be deeply sickening to you.)

The good:

[list]
[*] Combat feels weightier and animations are extremely polished and satisfying

[*] Visual effects such as flames and electricity are incredibly well made, and both effect and ambient lighting are gorgeous

[*] A lot of the core changes to things like skill gems, currency, and the passive tree successfully address many of the things I didn't enjoy about the first game

[*] Divisive as it is, I like the switch to more active, action-based combat, at least in concept. Blocking with shields, dodge rolling, etc. make the game feel more dynamic. In practice, though...
[/list]

The bad:

[list]
[*] Bosses suck. I'm sorry, but they do. The hard ones are miserable and the easy ones are boring. Having 80% of the arena slathered in lethal (but visually impressive!) elemental damage you may or may not be built to partially resist is a lame and anti-fun design choice. And it's unfortunately a VERY common mechanic. Most of them have gigantic health pools, too. So after you're done mowing down hordes of enemies and feeling like a badass, you can slowly chip away at this angry lightning man for 15 minutes while he shouts tropey villain quotes at you and then vaporizes you for flubbing a dodge roll.

[*] The entire game seems designed to punish melee combat. In the first game, you were basically forced to max out your defensive stats to an absurd degree if you wanted to play a tanky bruiser, but it was doable. In PoE2, every combat mechanic seems to be built around punishing you for even being in proximity to enemies. As someone who prefers up-close melee combat, the game just feels generally hostile towards my playstyle.

[*] Loot and quest rewards feel almost barren compared to PoE 1. They've purportedly made attempts to adjust this, but damn do I just feel so unrewarded most of the time. And vendors usually have mediocre inventory, so you can use all that gold to buy a blue-text weapon with bonuses to light radius and the wrong primary stat. Yeah, that sounds exciting. Sure.

[*] As with the first game, the community is awful. The most vocal ones are the usual bootlicking no-lifers with 7,000 hours who respond to every complaint about the game with "bro its so easy tho, just don't suck, the devs literally killed my family and cut off my arms and you don't hear ME whining about it". When guys like these are providing the bulk of the feedback the devs get, it kind of starts to explain how this game ended up being so frustrating.

[*] The hyper-expensive microtransaction model hasn't changed from the first game. 5 bucks for an item that lets you hide a piece of armor. A SINGLE piece of armor, on ONE character. Want more than one at a time? 5 more bucks. Want an armor set that doesn't look like drab garbage from the normal loot table? 40 bucks. Oh, but you can't toggle the annoying visual effect that comes with it. Obviously. Pay up, idiot.
[/list]

TL;DR Polished and good-looking but bosses suck, loot sucks, the community sucks, the MTX's suck, and the overall experience is more frustrating and unrewarding than its worth. Will it get better with time? It's possible. Will it get worse instead? Also possible. For now, I think I'll play something else.

Path of Exile 2 is shaping up to be one of the most ambitious ARPGs in years. Performance has been surprisingly stable, and the visual overhaul is stunning without feeling overwhelming. The soundtrack and sound design also deserve praise-every hit, spell, and monster roar lands with weight.

If you enjoyed Path of Exile 1 or simply love deep, loot-driven ARPGs, Path of Exile 2 is absolutely worth your time. It’s still evolving, but the foundation already feels extremely promising. I’m excited to see how the game grows from here.

[h2] Path of Exile 2[/h2]

From the very first minutes of the game, I was pleasantly surprised by the physics, movement quality, and combat mechanics in general. You could say that the visuals are no worse than Diablo 4 (and in some situations, even more interesting). 

Of course, the budget difference is colossal - one studio can literally create short films for its story - but for me, that's probably the only area where Diablo has the upper hand. If you want to chill and enjoy a cinematic storyline, that's the game for you.

But Path of Exile truly shines in battles against mobs and bosses - the sheer variety of builds and progression is insane. Almost every boss is unique in its own way, and this is the first Souls-like Diablo-style game I can remember (even though it loses some of that feel in the endgame).

The gameplay is pure excitement, and defeating mobs and bosses gives you a real dopamine rush - unlike the complete indifference I felt in Diablo 4. I want to wait for the full release and finish the remaining unfinished acts before diving into the endgame, but from what I’ve seen so far, I’m more than satisfied!

Enjoy a ranged game? sure, you might like it. Have any inclination to play a melee character? Don't bother. The entire game is designed with ranged in mind and GGG has failed, at least for me, to open up melee as a viable option.

Unfortunately, after almost 300 hours spent in this game, I've come to the conclusion that I can't really recommend it.

The honey moon phase is FANTASTIC. I've never played any other similar aRPGs, the Diablo games and the like nor the prequel, but despite the slightly overwhelming learning curve of the beginning I quickly became very addicted to this game. The campaign is fantastic and I enjoyed completing it many times with different kinds of builds that felt absolutely riveting to level up. For that experience alone I still hold this game in high regard. Someone somewhere said that learning is ultimately the best part in any videogame, and the amount you get to learn here to make yourself powerful feels really rewarding.

The problem is the endgame, and specifically one particular aspect of it that kills the game for me: loosing XP when dying. Now I get that there's got to be some kind of a consequence and punishment for dying (and playing badly), and there's arguably several here (loosing the Waystone and any items on the floor you didn't pick up), but the loss of the XP is just disrespectful to the player's time. Maybe I'd feel differently if I wasn't in my 30s now and felt like I'd have more time to dispose into gaming, but since that's not the case, this punishment feels horrendously frustrating. And it's not like I didn't try to min-max the heck out of the possibility of dying: I've watched several endgame build tutorials on how to stack defensive stats through leveling and gearing, spent hundreds and hundreds of exalted orbs onto really cracked gear, upgraded everything to the max and stacked resistances etc, but no matter what, sometimes you get deleted in seconds to some silly garbage you can't necessarily even see, which feels even more of a slap to my face. There's no out-learning the mechanics that kill me when sometimes I haven't the faintest clue what got me killed, and ofc you can't learn to avoid dying in something like a Souls-game by memorization since the maps, mobs and their modifiers are randomized etc. The Souls-games, generally considered very "unforgiving" are really nothing in comparison to this: in a Souls-game, you still get the chance to retrieve your potentially lost XP/currency (aside from Sekiro) if you end up messing up and dying, and 99% (if not 100%) of the time you're also able to play evasively and homeward out in order to make use of the souls (XP) in case you want to chicken out and not risk loosing your progress before tackling the new challenge. Slight tangent here comparing the experience to an entirely different kind of game, but the point is that POE 2 is frustratingly unforgiving with your time and effort to level up your character in the endgame, especially when the prospect of managing to get the next defensive or offensive node seems like the possible one that's going to help you survive a lot better in the future.

If they'll end up changing their minds about this and changing what punishment for dying in the endgame looks like, I'll be happy to re-install the game and to continue playing, but as for now, I'm REALLY not up for loosing progress again and again because of some nonsense. And I can't recommend you to play the game that far either; there's just better things to do with the time that you'll loose.
